HEADLINE: 'Mates' defy rail corruption inquiry
TEXT:
The covert videos showing envelopes containing $10,000 in cash being exchanged, the profanity-laden phone calls between rail executives joking about how best to get "a sprinkle" and the handwritten notes on how to use burner phones were shocking.

But it was the brazenness of explanations given under oath by James Pinder, the man who used to run Victoria's government-owned regional rail business V/Line, and George Haritos, the man who co-owns and runs Melbourne-based cleaning company Transclean that was breathtaking.

Victoria's Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (IBAC) this week demanded explanations from three men who described themselves as mates and "musketeers" as it documented allegations of corruption with videos and flow charts and tried to find out where there are deep institutional failings in the state's rail industry.

Both Mr Pinder, who was fired on Thursday by the Victorian government, and Mr Haritos insisted that tens of thousands of dollars in cash handed over by the Transclean CEO over the past few years were winnings from a remarkably successful gambling club formed between the two men that bet quadrellas on horses.

The cash, and an additional $320,000 in payments made by associates of Transclean that Mr Pinder used to help buy a house in Melbourne, came at the same time as Mr Pinder was in charge of extending an existing $17 million cleaning contract with Transclean by another $23 million.

Mr Pinder, who has run the $1 billion V/Line group since late 2016 and previously ran the rolling stock arm of Melbourne's Metro Trains, had only vague memories of most of the meetings and payments he was questioned about, frequently replying: "I don't remember."

IBAC Commissioner Robert Redlich, QC, showed his frustration with Mr Pinder's stonewalling on Tuesday afternoon after the former V/Line CEO said he didn't remember a conversation that included talk about "a sprinkle". Mr Redlich called for a 10-minute break and directed Mr Pinder's lawyer to talk to him.

IBAC counsel Paul Lawrie could barely hide his disbelief when listening to Mr Haritos' explanations of the purported gambling club that claimed to distribute its winnings from cash kept in a drawer of Mr Haritos' house.

"What you're saying, Mr Haritos, is that on 19 August, the day on which Mr Pinder had a search warrant executed on your house, that was the same day that you liquidated the pool from group 3 and paid him out precisely $10,000; is that what you're saying?" Mr Lawrie asked. Mr Haritos replied: "Correct."

On Friday, when it was put to Mr Haritos that there was no "gambling syndicate" and that "this is just a cover story to account for large cash payments you were making regularly to Mr Pinder", the Transclean CEO disagreed and said the money given to Mr Pinder was from the betting fund.

The gambling story appeared tenuous when Metro Trains operations manager Peter Bollas, who also lost his job this week, said he was given between $8000-$10,000 in cash most months by Transclean to ensure it kept its cleaning contracts and got awarded more work.

IBAC investigators found between $55,000 and $65,000 in cash at Mr Bollas' home when they searched it on August 19, 2020, bundled in $5000 and $10,000 packets. Most of it came from payments given by Mr Pinder or Mr Haritos, Mr Bollas told IBAC.

The "sprinkle" was a reference to plans to ask Mr Haritos for more money after both Metro Trains and V/Line gave Transclean extra work following the COVID-19 pandemic, Mr Bollas said.

COVID-19 was "an opportunity for us to throw you an extra bit of a you-know-what", Mr Pinder said to Mr Haritos in telephone called taped in early March. "They're talking about cleaning every train every three to six hours ... potentially it's an opportunity to, uh, do a little bit of boosting your coffers".

In late April, Mr Bollas complained to Mr Pinder Metro Trains was spending $1.3 million a month giving Transclean extra work due to COVID-19 (Mr Pinder said V/Line was spending $500,000 a month), but that Mr Haritos had not put more people on to clean trains.

Mr Bollas suggested to Mr Pinder he ask Mr Haritos for more money: "Tell him like this: 50 each ... We're not greedy f---rs but he needs to understand."

The "50" referred to asking for extra payments of $50,000 each, Mr Bollas told IBAC.

The public hearings have been adjourned until November 6.

HEADLINE: BHP's MacKenzie launches CEO school
TEXT:
An academy for aspiring chief executives looms as the latest extra-curricular activity for BHP chairman Ken MacKenzie.

Mr MacKenzie is the sole director and shareholder of a new company that was registered with ASIC last month under the name CEO Academy Pty Ltd.

The BHP chairman declined to comment on the venture, but it is understood the new company will facilitate work he will be doing with Melbourne Business School.

Mr MacKenzie is believed to be helping MBS with course material that will help foster future leaders, building on mentoring work he has been doing.

The new venture has no connection to the "CEO Academy" established in the United States by Korn Ferry vice-president Dennis Carey in concert with the Wharton Business School at the University of Pennsylvania.

That organisation spruiks itself as "the perfect war room training ground for newer CEOs and potential successors" and its events have been addressed by the likes of former Dow Chemical boss Andrew Liveris, former United Airlines chairman Glenn Tilton and former Verizon Communications boss Ivan Seidenberg.

It is unclear whether Mr MacKenzie's venture will hold similar events from its "principle place of business" in Sydney's Barangaroo International Towers - the same precinct that big corporates like Westpac and Origin Energy call home.

The new venture is expected to consume only a small number of days in Mr MacKenzie's diary each year, and comes after he was revealed in September to be involved with Australia's newest investment bank, Barrenjoey.

Departing BHP director Shriti Vadera told BHP shareholders earlier in October that Mr MacKenzie had sought permission from the BHP board before taking up his part-time role with Barrenjoey. Ms Vadera said Mr MacKenzie had also agreed to limits on his involvement with Barrenjoey.

"These include that BHP remains the chair's number-one priority at all times, that the position at Barrenjoey is part-time advisory and not executive, that Barrenjoey will not advise BHP, and that the chair himself will not advise on transactions or advise BHP competitors or our significant customers or suppliers," she told BHP's annual meeting of shareholders. "The board will continue to monitor potential conflicts on an ongoing basis and review them formally on an annual basis."

BHP has no formal connection to Mr MacKenzie's new CEO Academy, despite the address of BHP's global headquarters on Melbourne's Collins Street being given as Mr MacKenzie's address on the ASIC filings.

At 56, Mr MacKenzie remains relatively young by the standards of Australia's boardrooms, and his first two years as BHP chairman were spent working with a chief executive who was seven years older than him - Andrew Mackenzie.

The BHP chairman, who was chief executive of Amcor, is about three years older than BHP's new chief executive, Mike Henry.

Those close to Mr MacKenzie do not believe the extra-curricular activities are a sign that his time at BHP is nearing an end.

Mr MacKenzie is overseeing a significant turnover of the BHP board, with four directors leaving and four new directors joining over the past year.

That turnover has significantly reduced the average tenure of BHP directors from four years to two years over the past year.

HEADLINE: Survival test for shopping strips
TEXT:
Retail As Sydney's King Street revives, stores are still struggling.

Sydney's most bohemian neighbourhood and one of Australia's oldest, longest and busiest commercial strips has witnessed "survival of the fittest" since grinding to a halt under the COVID-19 lockdown in March.

The lockdown was a sudden departure from life as Newtown's King Street knew it. Thu Nguyen, the owner of Elise Boutique, which sells vintage-inspired designer clothing, lost sleep over the disappearance of her only source of income as her store's open sign spun to closed, with no time frame on when she would be able to reopen.

Elise Boutique was founded in 2004, with the shop moving to its current King Street premises 12 years ago. But the past few months have been Ms Nguyen's biggest struggle, forcing the closure of her Melbourne store in the Centreway Arcade on Collins Street, compelling her to let go of staff members and cut back on expenses, and all with little or no support from her King Street landlord.

"It's really tough, because the rent we started with for that store 12 years ago is $100,000 a year. But ... it increased to almost $150,000 a year. That's crazy for a small business. We asked for a reduction and he said, 'No, no, no.' We still have two years left on the lease, but after it is finished I will probably move to somewhere in King Street that's a bit cheaper," she said.

With Melbourne reopening following one of the world's longest and strictest COVID-19 lockdowns, shopkeepers will be looking to their Sydney counterparts for a sense of what to expect.

"I don't think it will be an amazing year," said Ms Nguyen. "September to January is usually the biggest season for us, but this year we're just taking it really easy. We don't expect more. We still open the door, we still have a business, we're happy with that."

Local resident and estate agent Emmanuel Loukis, of Wiseberry Enmore, says the name of the game on King Street is survival of the fittest.

"The rents have always been quite high and all the entry-level operators and even some premium operators have struggled along King Street, but COVID forced operators that were struggling to close," he said.

At a glance, Rowda Ya-Habibi a 42-year-old Lebanese restaurant, is now closed; factory outlet clothing store ClearIt closed on October 25; and down the south end, The House, a licensed cafe, is shut. "With the turnover of stock, the majority of my inquiries is with very experienced operators who already have two to three existing businesses," Mr Loukis said. "You're now going to see a higher calibre of tenant that has more experience than your average start-up."

Andrew Bozza, senior executive of Belle Property Commercial Inner West, said experienced operators were "out there in droves" looking at King Street, but added that the increased supply was not all due to COVID-19.

"The stock we are holding at the moment, the majority of them, COVID was not a factor in them winding up. They had already made a decision not to extend the lease, COVID just reinforced that," he said. 'There's a lot of multi-site operators coming in, saying this is our chance to secure something along King Street. Two years ago, there were barely any vacancies at all."

HEADLINE: Is the RBA blowing up a property price bubble?
TEXT:
A growing divergence between residential property prices and rents could mean the Reserve Bank's unprecedented rate cuts and expected quantitative easing are laying the groundwork for the country's next property bubble.

The International Monetary Fund's standard definition of a bubble is "a positive deviation of the market price from its fundamental value".

Fundamental value for property typically includes the income from rent. Official figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics released this week recorded falling rents across the country.

In Sydney, rents have either fallen or not grown for seven consecutive quarters. They are now down 3.1 per cent annually in the September quarter.

In the more volatile cities of Perth and Darwin, rents have either fallen or not grown for 23 consecutive quarters. In Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide and Hobart rents all fell.

Population growth, unemployment and supply will determine future rent.

At the same time, residential property prices are on the rise. They have been growing in most capital cities (except Sydney and Melbourne) despite the COVID-19 hit.

When CoreLogic reports its house price index on Sunday, it will show combined capital city prices actually will have risen in October for the first time since April.

Some commentators, such as AFR Weekend's Christopher Joye, say prices are about to jump 20 per cent.

More record monetary easing from the Reserve Bank is pushing billions of dollars of loans through commercial banks into the property market.

Investors have started responding. New investor loans for property - excluding refinancing - jumped 9.3 per cent month on month in August, according to the ABS.

SQM Research's Louis Christopher says there has clearly been a divergence between asset prices and yields. "I have real concerns over an asset price bubble forming," he said.

"We are in an unusual position of where an investor can now get a cash flow-positive property because of record low interest rates, and I have never seen that in Sydney before."

Economists such as former Federal Reserve board member Frederic Mishkin have argued that credit-fuelled asset price bubbles are more dangerous to financial stability and economic growth than bubbles without debt build-ups.

So why is the Reserve Bank not more concerned about such bubbles as it prepares to deliver more record monetary stimulus on Tuesday?

One key consideration is that residential property prices are not solely driven by rent. Much of property price growth can be driven by owner-occupiers, people seeking a place to live.

Second, the Reserve Bank doesn't see rates rising for at least three years so the serviceability - at least for those in work - won't be a problem.

Furthermore, the federal government has also provided grants and financial support for new properties. It is also likely to get bipartisan support for expanding immigration and population growth once COVID-19 restrictions abate. These things can all help balance the market.

Before COVID-19, the RBA's deputy governor, Guy Debelle, said a shortfall in housing supply was "quite likely" in the foreseeable future and that would trigger a "larger price response" in property values.

Higher prices from a supply shortage could be cancelled out by the weak population growth. If there is greater unemployment, there may be some marginal forced selling that could temper the price growth.

The benefits of higher house prices could also be through the so-called wealth effect, where people think they are richer because their house is worth more, so they increase spending.
